title: Weber-Barstow Maneuver | Functional Leg Length Difference
purpose: Screen for a functional leg length difference (compensation from positioning such as scoliosis or excessive foot pronation rather than structure).
structure: Medial malleoli compared after resetting the pelvis.
procedure: Patient supine; apply slight traction so both legs are positioned alike. Palpate the distal medial malleoli, have the patient flex hips and knees and lift the pelvis off the table, then passively extend the knees, bring the feet together and compare malleolar heights with the thumbs.

accuracy.source: Reliability only: Gomez-Aguilar et al. 2021 inter-rater kappa 0.52 (moderate)

notes: About 90% of people have a leg length inequality (mean 5.2 mm); anatomic inequality is usually not clinically significant until about 20 mm (Knutson 2005). Part of basic hip assessment with AROM and PROM.

title: Cluster of Sutlive | Hip Osteoarthritis Test Cluster
purpose: Five-item clinical prediction rule (Sutlive et al. 2008) for preliminary diagnosis of hip osteoarthritis in unilateral hip pain, reducing the need for radiographs and allowing early conservative management.
structure: Hip joint; radiographic reference is Kellgren-Lawrence grading.
procedure: 1) Positive hip scour test: supine, hip flexed 90°, moved toward the opposite shoulder with axial load through the femur, then internal rotation with compression and adduction with compression, assessing groin pain/symptoms. 2) Passive hip internal rotation ≤ 25° (prone, knee 90°, inclinometer proximal to the lateral malleolus, maximal IR until the contralateral buttock rises). 3) Hip pain with squatting. 4) Active hip flexion causes lateral pain. 5) Active hip extension is painful.
positive: 3 of 5 positive → LR+ 5.2; 4 of 5 → LR+ 24.3 (95% CI 4.4-142.1, use with caution).
notes: Page rates moderate clinical value. Related: Patrick's test, Trendelenburg sign, signs & symptoms of hip OA.

title: McCarthy Test | Femoroacetabular Impingement (FAI) Assessment
purpose: Test for hip labral pathology / FAI mentioned in several clinical-diagnosis papers.
procedure: Patient supine, both legs maximally flexed by the examiner; the patient holds the non-tested leg in full flexion. The examiner extends the tested leg first with external rotation, then again with internal rotation; repeat on the asymptomatic side.
positive: Reproduction of the patient's hip pain, with or without a click.

accuracy.source: n/a: never subjected to formal diagnostic accuracy studies (Springer et al. 2009 cited)

notes: Clinical value questionable. Related: Thomas test, anterior/posterior labral tear tests, FADDIR, foot progression angle walking test.

title: Foot Progression Angle Walking Test | FAI
purpose: Dynamic walking test (Ranawat et al. 2017) to reproduce activity-related symptoms of FAI (internal foot progression) or hip instability (external foot progression).
structure: Femoral head-neck junction abutment with internal rotation (FAI); undercoverage/instability with external rotation.
procedure: The patient walks normally with a neutral foot angle, then with the foot/leg internally rotated about 15° from neutral, then with external foot progression.
positive: Pain elicited with the altered foot progression angle, or exacerbation of baseline pain: internal FPAW positive in FAI, external FPAW positive in instability.

accuracy.source: Ranawat et al. 2017 (evaluated alongside FADIR and FABER)

notes: Poor likelihood ratios; weak clinical value pending validation. Related: Thomas, anterior/posterior labral tear tests, FADDIR, McCarthy.

title: HEER (Hyperextension-External Rotation) Test | Hip Microinstability
purpose: Assess hip microinstability (young patients) by hyperextension and external rotation.
structure: Hip stabilizers: acetabulum, labrum, ligamentum teres, capsuloligamentous complex, muscles; traumatic and atraumatic onsets; repetitive axial/rotational loading with anatomic abnormality.
procedure: Patient supine with the legs hanging over the end of the bench; the patient holds the unaffected leg flexed. The examiner hyperextends and externally rotates the affected leg.

accuracy.source: Hoppe et al. 2017 (first validity study, limitations)

notes: Moderate clinical value; combine with history and Beighton score. Related: prone instability test of the hip, AB-HEER, foot progression walking angle.

title: AB-HEER Test | Hip Microinstability Assessment
purpose: Assess hip microinstability by abduction-hyperextension-external rotation with an anterior force on the greater trochanter.
structure: Hip stabilizers (acetabulum, labrum, ligamentum teres, capsuloligamentous complex, muscles).
procedure: Patient lies on the unaffected side. The affected leg is abducted 30-45°, extended and externally rotated while the examiner applies an anteriorly directed force to the posterior greater trochanter.

accuracy.source: Hoppe et al. 2017 (first validity study, limitations)

notes: Moderate clinical value. Related: prone instability test of the hip, HEER, foot progression walking angle.

title: Kendall Test / Modified Thomas Test | Rectus Femoris Length
purpose: Assess rectus femoris length (modified Thomas test).
procedure: Patient supine with both legs off the end of the table; the patient pulls one knee to the chest and holds it. Test both sides; palpate to confirm rectus femoris tightness.
positive: The hanging leg rises and does not stay at 90° knee flexion.
notes: SOURCE NOTE: the page embeds the same YouTube ID as the Phelps test page (NDsPj1qATiU); verify which video plays. Related length tests: Ober's, Ely's, Phelps, 90-90 SLR, backsaver sit and reach, tripod sign, Thomas.

title: Backsaver Sit and Reach Test | Hamstring Length Assessment
purpose: Standardized hamstring length test, often used in research with a sit-and-reach box.
procedure: Sitting, one knee flexed against the chest to stabilize the pelvis, the other knee extended; the patient flexes the trunk and tries to touch the toes of the extended leg. Repeat on the other side.
positive: Unable to reach at least the toes = tight hamstrings.

accuracy.source: Reliability only: Ayala et al. 2012 intra-rater ICC 0.97; a change of 5.59° indicates real change

notes: Related length tests: Ober's, Ely's, Phelps, 90-90 SLR, Kendall, tripod sign, Thomas.

title: Greater Trochanter Palpation | Gluteal Tendinopathy (GTPS)
purpose: Palpation of the gluteus medius/minimus insertions for gluteal tendinopathy (greater trochanteric pain syndrome).
structure: Greater trochanter 'clock face' (Falvey et al.): gluteus medius and bursa at 12, gluteus minimus and bursa at 1, gluteus maximus 2-6 with vastus lateralis outside, quadratus femoris 7-8, conjoint gemelli/obturator internus 8-10, piriformis 10-11.
procedure: Patient on the unaffected side, hips flexed about 60°, knees together; palpate the structures around the greater trochanter, especially the gluteus medius/minimus insertions.
positive: Reproduction of the lateral hip pain of at least 2/10 NPRS on palpation of the gluteus medius/minimus insertions.

accuracy.source: Grimaldi et al. (text 2016, reference 2017), vs MRI; most sensitive test in that study

notes: Moderate clinical value for excluding gluteal tendinopathy. Other GTPS tests: resisted external derotation, single leg stance, FADER/FADER-R, ADD/ADD-R.

title: Resisted External Derotation Test | Gluteal Tendinopathy / GTPS
purpose: Test for gluteal tendinopathy (greater trochanteric pain syndrome).
structure: Gluteus medius/minimus tendons at the greater trochanter.
procedure: SOURCE ISSUE: the page's execution paragraph is copied from the Puranen-Orava page (standing hamstring stretch with the hip at 90°, knee extended, foot on the bench) and does not describe the resisted external derotation test; the actual execution (Lequesne 2008) is only shown in the video.
positive: Per the page text: exacerbation of the patient's familiar symptoms (copied wording).
notes: Page rates moderate clinical value despite the promising figures. Other GTPS tests: single leg stance, greater trochanter palpation, FADER/FADER-R, ADD/ADD-R.

title: FADER Test / FADER-R Test | Gluteal Tendinopathy (GTPS)
purpose: Flexion-ADduction-External Rotation test, with added resisted internal rotation (FADER-R), for gluteal tendinopathy.
structure: Gluteus medius/minimus tendons under tensile and compressive load.
procedure: Patient supine. Flex the hip to 90°, adduct and add external rotation to end range; then ask for isometric internal rotation against resistance (FADER-R).
positive: Reproduction of the lateral hip pain at the greater trochanter of at least 2/10 NPRS.

accuracy.source: Grimaldi et al. (text 2016, reference 2017), vs MRI

notes: A positive test raises confidence that gluteal tendinopathy is present; a negative test changes little. Moderate clinical value. Other GTPS tests: resisted external derotation, single leg stance, greater trochanter palpation, ADD/ADD-R.

title: ADD Test / ADD-R Test | Gluteal Tendinopathy (GTPS)
purpose: Passive hip adduction test (modified Ober's), with added resisted abduction (ADD-R), for gluteal tendinopathy.
structure: Gluteus medius/minimus tendons under passive and active tensile and compressive load.
procedure: Patient in diagonal side-lying on the unaffected side with the lower hip and knee flexed 80-90°; the affected leg supported with the knee extended, in line with the trunk, ASIS perpendicular to the table. Stabilize the pelvis and move the leg into end-range adduction with overpressure; then ask for isometric abduction against resistance (ADD-R).
positive: Reproduction of the lateral hip pain at the greater trochanter of at least 2/10 NPRS.

accuracy.source: Grimaldi et al. (text 2016, reference 2017), vs MRI; first study of this test

notes: Limited ability to exclude the condition; moderate clinical value. Other GTPS tests: resisted external derotation, single leg stance, greater trochanter palpation, FADER/FADER-R.

title: Heel Contralateral Knee Maneuver (HCLK) | Piriformis Syndrome
purpose: Provocation manoeuvre for deep gluteal syndrome (piriformis syndrome).
structure: Piriformis and sciatic nerve in the subgluteal space (same DGS background as the other piriformis pages).
procedure: Exclude lumbar spine and SIJ pathology first. Patient supine, externally rotates the tested hip and places the heel on the contralateral knee; the examiner flexes the contralateral hip. The position may need to be held for tens of seconds up to 1 minute.
positive: Reproduction of familiar gluteal pain and/or paraesthesia radiating into the posterior lower extremity.

accuracy.source: Michel et al. 2013 (DGS vs symptomatic L5/S1 disco-radicular conflict; reference standard unclear)

notes: Clinical utility questionable because the reference standard is unclear. Other DGS tests: Freiberg, Pace, seated piriformis stretch, FAIR, piriformis test, Beatty, active piriformis.

title: Long Stride Walking Test | Ischiofemoral Hip Impingement (IFI)
purpose: Walking test for ischiofemoral impingement (IFI), an extra-articular impingement between the lesser trochanter and the lateral ischium causing posterior hip pain.
structure: Ischiofemoral space (lateral ischium to lesser trochanter) and quadratus femoris space (lesser trochanter to proximal hamstring tendons), both reduced in IFI (Torriani et al. 2009); first described by Johnson 1977, still disputed. Pain lateral to the ischium at toe-off/pre-swing in terminal hip extension; sciatic nerve entrapment can cause radiating pain.
procedure: The patient walks with long strides (provoking impingement in terminal extension), then with short strides avoiding maximal extension.
positive: Posterior pain lateral to the ischium reproduced with long strides and relieved with short strides.

accuracy.source: Gómez-Hoyos et al. 2016 (retrospective; reference standard = posterior hip pain + MRI + ≥60% relief after decompression; reliability not assessed)

notes: Clinical value questionable for now (only study, retrospective). Companion: ischiofemoral impingement test. The differential-diagnosis graphic (Gómez-Hoyos 2018) is an image not in the API text.

title: Ischiofemoral Impingement Test | Ischiofemoral Hip Impingement
structure: Ischiofemoral and quadratus femoris spaces (see long stride walking test).
procedure: Patient side-lying on the unaffected side. The examiner palpates the lateral ischium with one hand and brings the affected hip into maximal extension in adduction or neutral; if familiar posterior pain appears, repeat with the hip in abduction.
positive: Familiar posterior hip pain reproduced in adduction/neutral extension but not in abduction.

accuracy.source: Gómez-Hoyos et al. 2016 (retrospective; combined reference standard; reliability not assessed)

notes: Clinical value questionable for now. Companion: long stride walking test.

title: Puranen-Orava Test | Proximal Hamstring Tendinopathy
purpose: Pain provocation test for chronic proximal hamstring tendinopathy in athletes.
structure: Proximal hamstring tendons at the ischial tuberosity.
procedure: Standing, the patient actively stretches the hamstrings with the hip flexed about 90°, knee fully extended and the foot supported on the bench.
positive: Exacerbation of the patient's familiar symptoms.

accuracy.source: Cacchio et al. 2012 (symptoms ≥ 6 months, expert diagnosis confirmed by MRI; intra- and inter-rater reliability > 0.8)

notes: Moderate clinical value; first and only study. Related: sign of the buttock, bent knee stretch, modified bent knee stretch.

title: Bent Knee Stretch Test | Proximal Hamstring Tendinopathy
purpose: Pain provocation test for chronic proximal hamstring tendinopathy.
procedure: Patient supine. The examiner maximally flexes the hip and knee, then slowly straightens the knee.
positive: Exacerbation of the patient's familiar symptoms.
notes: Moderate clinical value pending confirmation; first and only study. Page text ends with a leftover video sign-off sentence. Related: sign of the buttock, modified bent knee stretch, Puranen-Orava.

title: Modified Bent Knee Stretch Test | Proximal Hamstring Tendinopathy
purpose: Rapid-stretch variant for chronic proximal hamstring tendinopathy.
procedure: Patient supine with legs extended. The examiner holds the symptomatic leg behind the heel and at the knee, maximally flexes hip and knee, then rapidly straightens the knee.
positive: Exacerbation of the patient's familiar symptoms.
notes: Moderate clinical value pending confirmation; first and only study. Related: sign of the buttock, bent knee stretch, Puranen-Orava.

title: Sign of the Buttock | Proximal Hamstring Tendinopathy Assessment
purpose: Originally a screening sign for serious buttock pathology (ischial bursitis, neoplasm, abscess); also used for proximal hamstring tendinopathy.
procedure: Perform a straight leg raise; as soon as it is limited, flex the knee and check whether hip flexion can be increased further.
positive: Hip flexion cannot be increased with the knee flexed = positive sign of the buttock (ischial bursitis, neoplasm, abscess or hip pathology). Pain with further flexion suggests proximal hamstring tendinopathy.
notes: No references listed. Related: bent knee stretch, modified bent knee stretch, Puranen-Orava.
